dev_notes_primitives:
The model already had a believable driving desk, so this was repair work, not a rebuild. Three defects were doing all the damage. Both notch tracks were painted on a decal that the lever pivot housing sat on top of, so the detents existed and were invisible. The signalling screen was eleven millimetres behind the front face of its own bezel, so what everyone saw was dark metal, not a display. And the default framing cut at the desk apron, which threw the foot pedal out of shot and took two more criteria with it. I dropped each controller pivot 200 mm into the console, which gives a 250 mm travel and room for a real slot with a comb of notch steps on both sides, put the screen in front of its tray, and reframed from the panel hood down to the toe of the pedal.

Two things for whoever picks this up. Every detent lives in one array per controller, and the plate art, the teeth and the labels all rebuild from it, so adding a notch is one edit, not four. The gate boot follows the lever every frame instead of being parented to the arm, so if you change PIVOT_DROP the boot still lands in the right place. Camera home is a locked mark that the asset build reuses, so please do not retune it.
dev_notes_assets:
Same scene, same camera, same palette, same UI, rebuilt with real materials. It keeps the composition of the primitive object for object, including the horn plunger, the switch bank, the extinguisher, the route card and the heater grille, and it keeps the locked camera mark and the lit face on the left. What went up is mesh quality on the three hero parts, real PBR sets on everything else, a golden hour HDRI in place of the painted dome, and surface wear the procedural build could not carry.

Worth knowing: the scene is written from the same numbers as the web build rather than imported from it, so all 347 objects arrive named, in their own collection, and editable. Every printed surface, both dials, the signalling screen, the four gate half plates and each engraved label, is the exact pixels exported from the web build, so the text cannot drift between the two versions. The light was matched by measurement, not by eye: seven regions sampled in both delivery frames, six of them inside 9 per cent and the seventh at 15.

One declared difference. The video is 10 seconds rather than the usual 20, because that is the length that was asked for on this task.

All textures are CC0, from Poly Haven and ambientCG, so nothing needs crediting.

dev_notes_primitives:
The bench was nearly black and nothing on it moved, so a ratchet never got to show what it does. I put the tool on a pine top with a pegboard behind, drilled eight real wells into the tray, and stamped the size big on every socket end face so it reads from the opening view. The demo now runs by itself from the first second, turning the nut on the power stroke and holding the head still while the bar sweeps back.

For the dev: keep the gear group a child of the ratchet group with rotation driveAngle minus swing, that one line is what makes the head change angle against the bar.
dev_notes_assets:
Same bench, same camera, same eight sockets, same orange, only the making is better. The ratchet, the socket on the drive and the lamp are Meshy meshes, the five wrenches and the pliers on the board are Poly Haven scans, and every primitive that holds them up now carries a real texture map instead of a flat colour. Wood, rubber, plastic and steel come from ambientCG, retinted in the pixels so the palette lands on the primitive version, and the bench lamp throws a tight warm pool over the tray the same way the primitive does.

For the dev: every material is Image Texture, Normal Map, Principled and Output, tiling is baked into the UVs, the bench top runs 5 by 3.4 on its map, and EEVEE raytracing is switched off so the viewport plays back for the capture, turn it back on in Render Properties for a still render.
